## Hunks

### `historian/system.xml.md`

**ruling** (§11.17): Temporal and epistemic rules move into the base, so SWE inherits them: an anchor already dates every fact, a fact whose truth changes carries its validity bound, dates are absolute, and a claim nothing confirmed is written as a claim with its source. Placed after the facts rules; it applies to user observations as well. Part of the one historian re-validation batch.

```diff
@@ -411,2 +411,10 @@ Facts capture stable properties of the project that survive past any single comp
 
+### Time and certainty
+
+These rules apply to facts and to user observations.
+
+- **When something was said is already known.** Every fact keeps its anchor in the history, so do not add "as of" dates or the session date to a fact that stays true.
+- **A fact whose truth changes carries its validity.** When a fact holds only until a date or an event, write that bound into the fact: "Release freeze until 2026-11-02", "Staging uses the old signing key until the key migration finishes". This is the fact's validity, not chronology wording. When the end is unknown, write the fact without one; never guess a date.
+- **Absolute dates only.** Resolve "tomorrow", "next Friday" or "end of the month" to a calendar date (YYYY-MM-DD) from the dates the chunk shows. If the chunk does not show which date it means, keep the event or condition and leave the date out.
+- **Claimed or confirmed.** A statement that only someone asserted (the user, a teammate, a document or another agent) and that nothing in the chunk confirmed is written as a claim with its source: "Per the user, the vendor API allows 100 requests per minute". A fact that a tool result, test run, file or other direct evidence in the chunk confirmed is written plainly, and so is a rule or decision the user sets: the user saying it is what makes it true. Never turn a guess, plan or proposal into a confirmed fact.
 ### The 5 categories
```

**ruling** (§11.11): causal_incident regains the optional link to the CONSTRAINTS fact it produced, so that constraint carries its evidence from the start.

```diff
@@ -618,2 +626,3 @@ Optional:
 - `ord_span` — start-end ordinal range if narrower than the compartment
+- `produced_fact` — when this incident also produced a `CONSTRAINTS` fact in this output, that fact's exact text, so the constraint keeps this incident as its evidence
```

**ruling** (§11.13, §11.14, §11.15): The user-observation section is now the base's: observations go under a named user category (five base categories plus the two SWE user categories, definitions generated from the category declarations), mixed traits are split at extraction, and the SWE layer adds its split examples. 'Framework choices, coding language preferences' are no longer dropped; cross-project ones go to DEV_ENVIRONMENT. Sensitive details and facts about other people are excluded explicitly. The inline output example moved to the MC output section.

-## User observations (optional, experimental)
+## User observations (optional)

+After outputting compartments and facts, also output a `<user_observations>` section IF the chunk shows durable patterns about the human user. A separate review promotes patterns that recur across sessions into the user's profile, which this user's agents read in every later session, so precision matters more than recall.
 
-- User observations capture UNIVERSAL behavioral patterns about the human user — not project-specific or technical.
-- Good observations: communication preferences, review focus areas, expertise level, decision-making patterns, frustration triggers, working style.
-- Bad observations (DO NOT emit): project-specific preferences, framework choices, coding language preferences, one-off moods, task-local frustration.
-- Each observation must be a single concise, present-tense statement phrased verb-first without a subject.
-- Only emit observations you have strong evidence for from the conversation. Do not speculate. Zero observations is fine when nothing stands out.
-- The output shape gains an additional section:
-```
-<user_observations>
-* Prefers terse communication and dislikes verbose explanations.
-* Understands cache invalidation, SQLite internals, and prompt engineering.
-</user_observations>
-```
-If no observations, omit the `<user_observations>` section entirely.
+Each observation belongs to exactly one user category and is written inside that category's tag in the `<user_observations>` block (see Output). The user categories:
+
+#### `COMMUNICATION`
+
+**Test**: "Does this change how an agent should talk to the user — length, tone, format, language, or how much to explain?"
+
+How the user wants agents to communicate with them, in any kind of work: length and density, tone, structure of answers, how much to explain, the language to reply in, and how and when to ask questions.
+
+**Positive examples**:
+- "Prefers short answers with the conclusion first."
+- "Wants plain language without jargon in summaries."
+- "Expects one question at a time, not a list of questions."
+
+**Negative examples (do NOT extract as COMMUNICATION)**:
+- "Wants to review diffs rather than whole files" — only meaningful in one kind of work; it belongs to that domain's user category if the profile has one.
+- "Was curt in this session" — one-off mood.
+
+#### `PREFERENCES`
+
+**Test**: "Is this a like or dislike the user holds everywhere, one that should shape what an agent chooses or proposes?"
… 108 more lines; full text in rendered/historian/system.xml.md
```

**mc-interface** (§11.17): Turn two picks the decay class from the resolved profile's closed list (the base's six plus any a profile adds), generated from decay_classes. MC's turn-two parser validates the value and falls back to the category's default decay class. Same re-validation batch.

```diff
@@ -721,3 +845,9 @@ One decision per `fact_id`. Actions: `new`, `covered`, `conflict`, `edit`, `merg
 - Every removed, replaced and added clause cites a block start ordinal of that fact's own blocks and an exact excerpt.
-- `scores` is optional; absent means empty. Each score requires integer `item`, integer `importance` from 1 to 100, and `class`, a free nonempty string of at most 64 characters proposing a decay class. There is no decay-class taxonomy.
+- `scores` is optional; absent means empty. Each score requires integer `item`, integer `importance` from 1 to 100, and `class`, the item's decay class: exactly one of the ids below. A value outside that list is replaced by the default decay class of the item's category.
+  - `stable`: True until contradicted (a name, a standing boundary, a load-bearing design reason).
+  - `drifting`: Likely to change over months (tastes, current focus, tool choices, external limits that vendors lift).
+  - `bounded`: Has a known validity window; hidden after it ends, history kept.
+  - `recurring`: Repeats by rule; freshness follows the next occurrence.
+  - `open_until_resolved`: Commitments and situations; ends on a resolution event, never silently.
+  - `dated_permanent`: Past milestones; constant freshness.
```

+3. If a candidate is semantically equivalent to an existing stable memory, mark it as already covered.
+4. If multiple candidates describe the same trait, merge them into one clean statement.
+5. Never promote secrets, credentials, account numbers, or health, financial or relationship details, whatever category a candidate carries.
+6. Use only the user categories listed below; never invent a category.
+
+### User categories
+
+- **COMMUNICATION** (global; seen by every profile's agents) — how the user wants agents to talk to them in any work: length, tone, format, reply language, how much to explain.
+- **PREFERENCES** (global; seen by every profile's agents) — likes and dislikes the user holds everywhere, including design and visual taste.
+- **BOUNDARIES** (global; seen by every profile's agents) — what the user wants to confirm before an agent acts, and what they never want done.
+- **WORKING_STYLE** (global; seen by every profile's agents) — how the user works with agents whatever the task: pace, planning, review habits, decision style, feedback.
+- **IDENTITY** (global; seen by every profile's agents) — who the user is: name and form of address, time zone, languages, profession and current main focus.
+- **ENGINEERING_PRACTICE** (global; seen by only agents running @cortexkit/memory-swe) — how the user does and wants software engineering done in every codebase: debugging, testing, review, delivery, agent workflow.
+- **DEV_ENVIRONMENT** (global; seen by only agents running @cortexkit/memory-swe) — the user's own development setup shared by their coding projects: stack, runtimes, package managers, editor, shell, OS.
+
+### Category instructions
+
+1. Only promote traits that hold across the user's work. A preference tied to one project belongs to that project's memory, not here: dismiss it.
+2. Put each promoted trait in the one user category whose test it passes. A candidate that mixes a general trait with a domain-specific one is promoted as two memories, one per category.
+3. Do NOT promote: one-off moods, task-local frustrations, or anything about other people.
+4. Phrase every promoted or updated memory as a concise, present-tense verb-first statement without a subject (for example, "Prefers concise explanations" or "Expects changes to be tested").
+5. If an existing stable memory should be updated based on new evidence, include the update and keep the same verb-first, subjectless phrasing and its category.
+
+### Software categories
+
+- `ENGINEERING_PRACTICE` and `DEV_ENVIRONMENT` traits follow the same rules. Framework, language and tool preferences qualify when the candidates come from more than one project; when they all come from one project, dismiss them as project-specific.
+- Split a candidate that mixes an engineering practice with a general trait the way the historian does: the general part under its base category, the engineering part under `ENGINEERING_PRACTICE`.
